query: For a FeNiCrCoCu high-entropy alloy used as a thin coating on a conventional metal substrate, what single testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain what governs overall wear resistance and microscopic deformation during sliding in the intended high-temperature operating regime? Define a controlled change relative to a baseline coating condition, predict the corresponding directional changes in wear and deformation, state the regime in which those predictions should hold, identify supporting prior evidence, and specify a result that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: Under high-temperature sliding conditions, the overall wear resistance and microscopic deformation of a FeNiCrCoCu high-entropy alloy coating are governed by the in situ formation of a protective Cr‐rich oxide tribolayer. This layer, generated via preferential oxidation of Cr at elevated temperatures in air, reduces local shear stresses and retards plastic deformation by acting as a load-bearing, low-friction interface.
generation.material_initial_state: A baseline FeNiCrCoCu high-entropy alloy coating deposited as a thin, uniform, and fully dense layer on a conventional metal substrate (without any specialized pre-oxidation or surface treatment).
generation.intervention: Subject a set of identical coatings to a controlled pre-oxidation treatment—exposure at high temperature to oxidizing air (for example, heating at 600°C for 30 minutes) prior to sliding tests—to promote the formation and stabilization of a Cr‐rich oxide tribolayer.
generation.conditions: Wear testing under sliding conditions in air at elevated temperatures (e.g., 600°C) with controlled load and sliding speed over a set duration.
generation.structural_mediator: A thin, adherent, Cr‐rich oxide film that forms at the wear interface.
generation.mechanism: The intervention accelerates the selective oxidation of Cr, creating an oxide layer that reduces interfacial shear and acts as a barrier to direct metal–metal contact. This protective film minimizes abrasive and adhesive wear while reducing the extent of plastic (microscopic) deformation in the substrate.
generation.predicted_outcome: Relative to the baseline (untreated) coating, the pre-oxidized coating will exhibit a lower wear rate, smoother wear track profiles, reduced friction coefficient, and less evidence of severe plastic deformation during sliding tests.
generation.baseline: The as-deposited coating without pre-oxidation treatment, in which any oxide formation during wear is less controlled and does not yield a deliberately enriched Cr‐rich layer.
generation.boundary: This mechanism is expected to hold under high-temperature, oxidative sliding conditions (e.g., around 600°C in air). The protective effect of the oxide tribolayer may not manifest under room-temperature or inert atmosphere conditions.
generation.uncertainty: While there is a plausible basis for selective Cr oxidation in similar high-entropy alloys, the extent of Cr segregation and the precise composition, thickness, and durability of the oxide tribolayer under these specific processing and test conditions require further microstructural verification.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of FeNiCrCoCu coatings under identical deposition conditions. Subject one set to the pre-oxidation treatment (600°C in air for 30 minutes) while leaving the other set untreated. Then, perform sliding wear tests at 600°C in air using identical load, sliding speed, and duration parameters. Analyze the surfaces post-test using microscopy (e.g., SEM, TEM) and chemical analysis (e.g., XPS, EDS) to compare oxide layer formation, composition, and wear/deformation characteristics.
measurements: Wear rate (volume loss per sliding distance)
Surface and cross-sectional oxide layer composition and thickness
Microscopic features of plastic deformation (e.g., slip bands, grain size changes)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the pre-oxidized coatings do not exhibit a statistically significant improvement (lower wear rate, lower friction, reduced plastic deformation) compared to the baseline, or if the oxide layer does not show enrichment in Cr relative to the untreated coating, then the hypothesis will be considered falsified.
